Right-triangle ratios

Sine, cosine, tangent

sin⁡θ=opphyp\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}sinθ=hypopp​cos⁡θ=adjhyp\cos\theta = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}cosθ=hypadj​tan⁡θ=oppadj\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}tanθ=adjopp​

The idea

In a right triangle, pick one acute angle θ\thetaθ. The side across from it is the opposite, the side touching it is the adjacent, the longest side is the hypotenuse. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent (SOH CAH TOA). The ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.

Worked example

Triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 and θ\thetaθ opposite the side 3: sin⁡θ=35\sin\theta = \tfrac35sinθ=53​, cos⁡θ=45\cos\theta = \tfrac45cosθ=54​, tan⁡θ=34\tan\theta = \tfrac34tanθ=43​. A ladder of length 6 leaning at 60∘60^\circ60∘ reaches a height 6sin⁡60∘=336\sin 60^\circ = 3\sqrt36sin60∘=33​.

Reciprocal ratios

cot⁡θ=1tan⁡θ\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}cotθ=tanθ1​sec⁡θ=1cos⁡θ\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}secθ=cosθ1​csc⁡θ=1sin⁡θ\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}cscθ=sinθ1​

Symbols: cot⁡\cotcot: cotangent, sec⁡\secsec: secant, csc⁡\csccsc: cosecant.

The idea

Cotangent, secant and cosecant are just one over tangent, cosine and sine. Nothing new to learn: compute the basic ratio, then flip it. They blow up where the basic ratio is 0.

Worked example

At 60∘60^\circ60∘: cos⁡=12\cos = \tfrac12cos=21​ so sec⁡=2\sec = 2sec=2; sin⁡=32\sin = \tfrac{\sqrt3}2sin=23​​ so csc⁡=23\csc = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}csc=3​2​; tan⁡=3\tan = \sqrt3tan=3​ so cot⁡=13\cot = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}cot=3​1​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Complementary angles

sin⁡(90∘−θ)=cos⁡θ\sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\thetasin(90∘−θ)=cosθtan⁡(90∘−θ)=1tan⁡θ\tan(90^\circ - \theta) = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}tan(90∘−θ)=tanθ1​

The idea

The two acute angles of a right triangle add up to 90∘90^\circ90∘. The side opposite one of them is adjacent to the other, so the sine of one angle is the cosine of the other — that is where the “co” in cosine comes from.

Worked example

cos⁡50∘=sin⁡40∘\cos 50^\circ = \sin 40^\circcos50∘=sin40∘ and tan⁡70∘⋅tan⁡20∘=1\tan 70^\circ\cdot\tan 20^\circ = 1tan70∘⋅tan20∘=1. Spotting complementary pairs often makes an expression collapse to a number.

The unit circle

Coordinates of the point

P=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)P = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)P=(cosθ,sinθ)tan⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}tanθ=cosθsinθ​

Symbols: PPP: the point of the circle of radius 1 at angle θ\thetaθ from the positive xxx-axis.

The idea

Turn by the angle θ\thetaθ from the positive xxx-axis on a circle of radius 1. The point you reach has coordinates (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)(cosθ,sinθ): cosine is the horizontal part (orange), sine the vertical part (pink). This works for every angle, not only acute ones.

Worked example

At 120∘120^\circ120∘ the point is in the second quadrant, mirrored from 60∘60^\circ60∘: (−12,32)(-\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}2)(−21​,23​​). So cos⁡120∘=−12\cos 120^\circ = -\tfrac12cos120∘=−21​, sin⁡120∘=32\sin 120^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}2sin120∘=23​​ and tan⁡120∘=−3\tan 120^\circ = -\sqrt3tan120∘=−3​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Pythagorean identities

sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1sin2θ+cos2θ=11+tan⁡2θ=1cos⁡2θ1 + \tan^2\theta = \frac{1}{\cos^2\theta}1+tan2θ=cos2θ1​

The idea

The point (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)(cosθ,sinθ) is on the circle of radius 1, so by Pythagoras cos⁡2θ+sin⁡2θ=1\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1cos2θ+sin2θ=1. Dividing by cos⁡2θ\cos^2\thetacos2θ gives the second identity. Use them to find one ratio from another; the quadrant decides the sign.

Worked example

sin⁡θ=35\sin\theta = \tfrac35sinθ=53​ with θ\thetaθ in the second quadrant: cos⁡2θ=1−925=1625\cos^2\theta = 1 - \tfrac{9}{25} = \tfrac{16}{25}cos2θ=1−259​=2516​, and cosine is negative there, so cos⁡θ=−45\cos\theta = -\tfrac45cosθ=−54​ and tan⁡θ=−34\tan\theta = -\tfrac34tanθ=−43​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Signs by quadrant

I:sin⁡,cos⁡,tan⁡>0\text{I}: \sin, \cos, \tan > 0I:sin,cos,tan>0II:sin⁡>0\text{II}: \sin > 0II:sin>0III:tan⁡>0\text{III}: \tan > 0III:tan>0IV:cos⁡>0\text{IV}: \cos > 0IV:cos>0

Symbols: I, II, III, IV: the four quadrants, counted anticlockwise from the top right.

The idea

Cosine is the xxx-coordinate and sine the yyy-coordinate, so their signs follow the quadrant. Tangent is their quotient: positive when both have the same sign (I and III). A memory aid: “All Students Take Calculus” — All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine are positive in quadrants I, II, III, IV.

Worked example

θ=300∘\theta = 300^\circθ=300∘ is in quadrant IV: cosine positive, sine and tangent negative. Indeed cos⁡300∘=12\cos 300^\circ = \tfrac12cos300∘=21​, sin⁡300∘=−32\sin 300^\circ = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}2sin300∘=−23​​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Periods

sin⁡,cos⁡: 2π\sin, \cos:\ 2\pisin,cos: 2πtan⁡: π\tan:\ \pitan: π

The idea

A full turn (2π2\pi2π) brings you back to the same point, so sine and cosine repeat every 2π2\pi2π. Tangent already repeats after half a turn, because the opposite point has both signs flipped. Inside, sin⁡(ωx)\sin(\omega x)sin(ωx) squeezes the graph: its period is 2πω\tfrac{2\pi}{\omega}ω2π​.

Worked example

sin⁡(3x)\sin(3x)sin(3x) has period 2π3\tfrac{2\pi}{3}32π​: three full waves fit in [0,2π][0, 2\pi][0,2π]. tan⁡(x+π)=tan⁡x\tan(x + \pi) = \tan xtan(x+π)=tanx, so a tangent graph repeats every π\piπ.

Degrees

0∘, 30∘, 45∘, 60∘, 90∘, 180∘0^\circ,\ 30^\circ,\ 45^\circ,\ 60^\circ,\ 90^\circ,\ 180^\circ0∘, 30∘, 45∘, 60∘, 90∘, 180∘

The idea

Half a turn is 180∘=π180^\circ = \pi180∘=π radians. So multiply degrees by π180\tfrac{\pi}{180}180π​ to get radians, and radians by 180π\tfrac{180}{\pi}π180​ to get degrees. Learn the key angles in both: 30∘=π630^\circ = \tfrac\pi630∘=6π​, 45∘=π445^\circ = \tfrac\pi445∘=4π​, 60∘=π360^\circ = \tfrac\pi360∘=3π​, 90∘=π290^\circ = \tfrac\pi290∘=2π​.

Worked example

225∘=225⋅π180=5π4225^\circ = 225\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{180} = \tfrac{5\pi}{4}225∘=225⋅180π​=45π​, and 7π6=7⋅180∘6=210∘\tfrac{7\pi}{6} = \tfrac{7\cdot 180^\circ}{6} = 210^\circ67π​=67⋅180∘​=210∘.

15° and 75°

sin⁡15∘=6−24\sin 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt6 - \sqrt2}{4}sin15∘=46​−2​​cos⁡15∘=6+24\cos 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}{4}cos15∘=46​+2​​

The idea

15∘=45∘−30∘15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ15∘=45∘−30∘ and 75∘=45∘+30∘75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ75∘=45∘+30∘, so the addition formulas give their exact values from the values you already know. Note sin⁡75∘=cos⁡15∘\sin 75^\circ = \cos 15^\circsin75∘=cos15∘ (complementary angles).

Worked example

cos⁡15∘=cos⁡45∘cos⁡30∘+sin⁡45∘sin⁡30∘=22⋅32+22⋅12=6+24≈0.966\cos 15^\circ = \cos 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ + \sin 45^\circ\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}2\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}{4} \approx 0.966cos15∘=cos45∘cos30∘+sin45∘sin30∘=22​​⋅23​​+22​​⋅21​=46​+2​​≈0.966.

Symmetries

Negative angle

sin⁡(−x)=−sin⁡x\sin(-x) = -\sin xsin(−x)=−sinxcos⁡(−x)=cos⁡x\cos(-x) = \cos xcos(−x)=cosxtan⁡(−x)=−tan⁡x\tan(-x) = -\tan xtan(−x)=−tanx

The idea

Turning clockwise by xxx gives the mirror image of turning anticlockwise: the point flips across the xxx-axis. Its xxx-coordinate stays (cosine is even), its yyy-coordinate changes sign (sine is odd), and so does the tangent.

Worked example

cos⁡(−π4)=22\cos(-\tfrac\pi4) = \tfrac{\sqrt2}2cos(−4π​)=22​​ and sin⁡(−π6)=−12\sin(-\tfrac\pi6) = -\tfrac12sin(−6π​)=−21​. The graph of cosine is symmetric about the yyy-axis; the graph of sine is symmetric about the origin.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Supplementary angle

sin⁡(π−x)=sin⁡x\sin(\pi - x) = \sin xsin(π−x)=sinxcos⁡(π−x)=−cos⁡x\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos xcos(π−x)=−cosx

The idea

π−x\pi - xπ−x is the mirror of xxx across the yyy-axis: same height, opposite horizontal position. So the sine is the same and the cosine changes sign. This is why sin⁡x=a\sin x = asinx=a usually has two solutions in [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π).

Worked example

sin⁡150∘=sin⁡30∘=12\sin 150^\circ = \sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12sin150∘=sin30∘=21​ and cos⁡150∘=−cos⁡30∘=−32\cos 150^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}2cos150∘=−cos30∘=−23​​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Half turn

sin⁡(x+π)=−sin⁡x\sin(x + \pi) = -\sin xsin(x+π)=−sinxcos⁡(x+π)=−cos⁡x\cos(x + \pi) = -\cos xcos(x+π)=−cosxtan⁡(x+π)=tan⁡x\tan(x + \pi) = \tan xtan(x+π)=tanx

The idea

Adding π\piπ sends the point to the opposite side of the circle: both coordinates change sign. Sine and cosine flip, but their quotient, the tangent, stays the same — that is why tangent has period π\piπ.

Worked example

sin⁡4π3=sin⁡(π3+π)=−32\sin\tfrac{4\pi}{3} = \sin(\tfrac\pi3 + \pi) = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}2sin34π​=sin(3π​+π)=−23​​ and tan⁡4π3=tan⁡π3=3\tan\tfrac{4\pi}3 = \tan\tfrac\pi3 = \sqrt3tan34π​=tan3π​=3​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Quarter turn

sin⁡(x+π2)=cos⁡x\sin\left(x + \tfrac\pi2\right) = \cos xsin(x+2π​)=cosxcos⁡(x+π2)=−sin⁡x\cos\left(x + \tfrac\pi2\right) = -\sin xcos(x+2π​)=−sinx

The idea

Shifting by π2\tfrac\pi22π​ turns the radius a quarter turn, which swaps the roles of the coordinates. On the graphs: the sine curve shifted left by π2\tfrac\pi22π​ is exactly the cosine curve.

Worked example

sin⁡(x+π2)+sin⁡(x−π2)=cos⁡x−cos⁡x=0\sin(x + \tfrac\pi2) + \sin(x - \tfrac\pi2) = \cos x - \cos x = 0sin(x+2π​)+sin(x−2π​)=cosx−cosx=0, since sin⁡(x−π2)=−cos⁡x\sin(x - \tfrac\pi2) = -\cos xsin(x−2π​)=−cosx.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Sum and difference

Sine

sin⁡(a±b)=sin⁡acos⁡b±cos⁡asin⁡b\sin(a \pm b) = \sin a\cos b \pm \cos a\sin bsin(a±b)=sinacosb±cosasinb

The idea

The sine of a sum is not the sum of sines. It mixes both functions: “sine-cosine plus cosine-sine”, with the same sign as in a±ba \pm ba±b. Typical use: new exact values (75∘=45∘+30∘75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ75∘=45∘+30∘) or combining two known angles.

Worked example

sin⁡75∘=sin⁡45∘cos⁡30∘+cos⁡45∘sin⁡30∘=22⋅32+22⋅12=6+24\sin 75^\circ = \sin 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ + \cos 45^\circ\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}2\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}4sin75∘=sin45∘cos30∘+cos45∘sin30∘=22​​⋅23​​+22​​⋅21​=46​+2​​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Cosine

cos⁡(a±b)=cos⁡acos⁡b∓sin⁡asin⁡b\cos(a \pm b) = \cos a\cos b \mp \sin a\sin bcos(a±b)=cosacosb∓sinasinb

The idea

For cosine the products pair like with like — “cosine-cosine, sine-sine” — and the sign is the opposite of the one in a±ba \pm ba±b. Setting a=ba = ba=b gives the double-angle formula.

Worked example

cos⁡15∘=cos⁡(45∘−30∘)=cos⁡45∘cos⁡30∘+sin⁡45∘sin⁡30∘=6+24\cos 15^\circ = \cos(45^\circ - 30^\circ) = \cos 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ + \sin 45^\circ\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}{4}cos15∘=cos(45∘−30∘)=cos45∘cos30∘+sin45∘sin30∘=46​+2​​: the minus inside became a plus.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Tangent

tan⁡(a±b)=tan⁡a±tan⁡b1∓tan⁡atan⁡b\tan(a \pm b) = \frac{\tan a \pm \tan b}{1 \mp \tan a\tan b}tan(a±b)=1∓tanatanbtana±tanb​

The idea

Divide the sine formula by the cosine formula and then divide top and bottom by cos⁡acos⁡b\cos a\cos bcosacosb: only tangents remain. Useful when you know tangents (slopes!) — the angle between two lines comes from this formula.

Worked example

tan⁡75∘=tan⁡(45∘+30∘)=1+131−13=3+13−1=2+3\tan 75^\circ = \tan(45^\circ + 30^\circ) = \dfrac{1 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}}{1 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt3 + 1}{\sqrt3 - 1} = 2 + \sqrt3tan75∘=tan(45∘+30∘)=1−3​1​1+3​1​​=3​−13​+1​=2+3​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Double and half angles

Double angle

sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos xsin2x=2sinxcosxtan⁡2x=2tan⁡x1−tan⁡2x\tan 2x = \frac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x}tan2x=1−tan2x2tanx​

The idea

Put b=ab = ab=a in the addition formulas. sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos xsin2x=2sinxcosx — not 2sin⁡x2\sin x2sinx: the graph of sin⁡2x\sin 2xsin2x is squeezed horizontally, not stretched vertically.

Worked example

sin⁡x=35\sin x = \tfrac35sinx=53​ with xxx acute: cos⁡x=45\cos x = \tfrac45cosx=54​, so sin⁡2x=2⋅35⋅45=2425\sin 2x = 2\cdot\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac45 = \tfrac{24}{25}sin2x=2⋅53​⋅54​=2524​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Cosine of a double angle

cos⁡2x=cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x=2cos⁡2x−1=1−2sin⁡2x\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 xcos2x=cos2x−sin2x=2cos2x−1=1−2sin2x

The idea

cos⁡2x=cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 xcos2x=cos2x−sin2x, and replacing one square with sin⁡2+cos⁡2=1\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1sin2+cos2=1 gives two more versions. Choose the one that uses what you know: only cos⁡x\cos xcosx, only sin⁡x\sin xsinx, or both.

Worked example

If sin⁡x=13\sin x = \tfrac13sinx=31​: cos⁡2x=1−2⋅19=79\cos 2x = 1 - 2\cdot\tfrac19 = \tfrac79cos2x=1−2⋅91​=97​ — no need to find cos⁡x\cos xcosx at all.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Lowering the power

sin⁡2x=1−cos⁡2x2\sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}sin2x=21−cos2x​cos⁡2x=1+cos⁡2x2\cos^2 x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}cos2x=21+cos2x​

The idea

Solve the double-angle formula for sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x or cos⁡2x\cos^2 xcos2x: a square becomes a first power of cos⁡2x\cos 2xcos2x. This is how you integrate sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x, and how you find half-angle values like cos⁡π8\cos\tfrac\pi8cos8π​.

Worked example

sin⁡2π12=1−cos⁡π62=1−322=2−34\sin^2\tfrac\pi{12} = \dfrac{1 - \cos\tfrac\pi6}{2} = \dfrac{1 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}2}{2} = \dfrac{2 - \sqrt3}{4}sin212π​=21−cos6π​​=21−23​​​=42−3​​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Triple angle

sin⁡3x=3sin⁡x−4sin⁡3x\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 xsin3x=3sinx−4sin3xcos⁡3x=4cos⁡3x−3cos⁡x\cos 3x = 4\cos^3 x - 3\cos xcos3x=4cos3x−3cosx

The idea

Write 3x=2x+x3x = 2x + x3x=2x+x, use the addition formula, then the double-angle formulas and cos⁡2=1−sin⁡2\cos^2 = 1 - \sin^2cos2=1−sin2. The result depends on sin⁡x\sin xsinx alone (or cos⁡x\cos xcosx alone): a cubic.

Worked example

Check with x=60∘x = 60^\circx=60∘: cos⁡x=12\cos x = \tfrac12cosx=21​, so cos⁡3x=4⋅18−32=−1\cos 3x = 4\cdot\tfrac18 - \tfrac32 = -1cos3x=4⋅81​−23​=−1, and indeed cos⁡180∘=−1\cos 180^\circ = -1cos180∘=−1.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

In terms of t = tan(x/2)

sin⁡x=2t1+t2\sin x = \frac{2t}{1 + t^2}sinx=1+t22t​cos⁡x=1−t21+t2\cos x = \frac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}cosx=1+t21−t2​

The idea

With t=tan⁡x2t = \tan\tfrac x2t=tan2x​, sine, cosine and tangent of xxx become fractions in ttt. It turns any trigonometric equation or integral in sin⁡x\sin xsinx, cos⁡x\cos xcosx into an algebraic one.

Worked example

t=1t = 1t=1 means x2=π4\tfrac x2 = \tfrac\pi42x​=4π​, so x=π2x = \tfrac\pi2x=2π​: the formulas give sin⁡x=22=1\sin x = \tfrac22 = 1sinx=22​=1 and cos⁡x=0\cos x = 0cosx=0, as they should.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Sums and products

Sum to product

sin⁡a+sin⁡b=2sin⁡a+b2cos⁡a−b2\sin a + \sin b = 2\sin\frac{a + b}{2}\cos\frac{a - b}{2}sina+sinb=2sin2a+b​cos2a−b​

The idea

A sum of two sines becomes a product: twice the sine of the average times the cosine of the half-difference. Products are what you want when solving equations (A⋅B=0A\cdot B = 0A⋅B=0 splits into two easy cases).

Worked example

sin⁡3x+sin⁡x=2sin⁡2xcos⁡x\sin 3x + \sin x = 2\sin 2x\cos xsin3x+sinx=2sin2xcosx. So sin⁡3x+sin⁡x=0\sin 3x + \sin x = 0sin3x+sinx=0 splits into sin⁡2x=0\sin 2x = 0sin2x=0 or cos⁡x=0\cos x = 0cosx=0.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

cos⁡a+cos⁡b=2cos⁡a+b2cos⁡a−b2\cos a + \cos b = 2\cos\frac{a + b}{2}\cos\frac{a - b}{2}cosa+cosb=2cos2a+b​cos2a−b​cos⁡a−cos⁡b=−2sin⁡a+b2sin⁡a−b2\cos a - \cos b = -2\sin\frac{a + b}{2}\sin\frac{a - b}{2}cosa−cosb=−2sin2a+b​sin2a−b​

The idea

The cosine versions follow the same pattern. Sum of cosines: cosine of the average times cosine of the half-difference. A product of cosines turns into half the sum of the cosines of the difference and the sum — the trick used to integrate products.

Worked example

cos⁡75∘+cos⁡15∘=2cos⁡45∘cos⁡30∘=2⋅22⋅32=62\cos 75^\circ + \cos 15^\circ = 2\cos 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ = 2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2 = \tfrac{\sqrt6}2cos75∘+cos15∘=2cos45∘cos30∘=2⋅22​​⋅23​​=26​​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Product to sum

sin⁡acos⁡b=12[sin⁡(a+b)+sin⁡(a−b)]\sin a\cos b = \tfrac12\left[\sin(a + b) + \sin(a - b)\right]sinacosb=21​[sin(a+b)+sin(a−b)]

The idea

The reverse direction: a product sin⁡acos⁡b\sin a\cos bsinacosb becomes half the sum of sin⁡(a+b)\sin(a + b)sin(a+b) and sin⁡(a−b)\sin(a - b)sin(a−b). It is exactly the sum of the two addition formulas. You need it to integrate sin⁡3xcos⁡x\sin 3x\cos xsin3xcosx and similar products.

Worked example

sin⁡75∘cos⁡15∘=12[sin⁡90∘+sin⁡60∘]=12(1+32)=2+34\sin 75^\circ\cos 15^\circ = \tfrac12[\sin 90^\circ + \sin 60^\circ] = \tfrac12\left(1 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right) = \tfrac{2 + \sqrt3}{4}sin75∘cos15∘=21​[sin90∘+sin60∘]=21​(1+23​​)=42+3​​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

cos⁡acos⁡b=12[cos⁡(a−b)+cos⁡(a+b)]\cos a\cos b = \tfrac12\left[\cos(a - b) + \cos(a + b)\right]cosacosb=21​[cos(a−b)+cos(a+b)]sin⁡asin⁡b=12[cos⁡(a−b)−cos⁡(a+b)]\sin a\sin b = \tfrac12\left[\cos(a - b) - \cos(a + b)\right]sinasinb=21​[cos(a−b)−cos(a+b)]

The idea

The cosine versions follow the same pattern. Sum of cosines: cosine of the average times cosine of the half-difference. A product of cosines turns into half the sum of the cosines of the difference and the sum — the trick used to integrate products.

Worked example

cos⁡75∘+cos⁡15∘=2cos⁡45∘cos⁡30∘=2⋅22⋅32=62\cos 75^\circ + \cos 15^\circ = 2\cos 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ = 2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2 = \tfrac{\sqrt6}2cos75∘+cos15∘=2cos45∘cos30∘=2⋅22​​⋅23​​=26​​.

Solving triangles

Law of sines

asin⁡A=bsin⁡B=csin⁡C=2R\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} = 2RsinAa​=sinBb​=sinCc​=2R

Symbols: aaa, bbb, ccc: the sides opposite the angles AAA, BBB, CCC; RRR: the radius of the circle through the three vertices (circumradius).

The idea

In any triangle each side is proportional to the sine of the opposite angle, and the common ratio is the diameter 2R2R2R of the circumscribed circle. Use it when you know an angle and its opposite side, plus one more side or angle.

Worked example

A=30∘A = 30^\circA=30∘, B=45∘B = 45^\circB=45∘, a=4a = 4a=4: b=asin⁡Bsin⁡A=4⋅2212=42b = \dfrac{a\sin B}{\sin A} = \dfrac{4\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}2}{\tfrac12} = 4\sqrt2b=sinAasinB​=21​4⋅22​​​=42​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Law of cosines

c2=a2+b2−2abcos⁡Cc^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos Cc2=a2+b2−2abcosC

Symbols: CCC: the angle between sides aaa and bbb, opposite side ccc.

The idea

Pythagoras with a correction term: c2=a2+b2−2abcos⁡Cc^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos Cc2=a2+b2−2abcosC. When C=90∘C = 90^\circC=90∘ the correction vanishes. Use it when you know two sides and the angle between them (SAS), or all three sides.

Worked example

a=5a = 5a=5, b=8b = 8b=8, C=60∘C = 60^\circC=60∘: c2=25+64−2⋅5⋅8⋅12=49c^2 = 25 + 64 - 2\cdot 5\cdot 8\cdot\tfrac12 = 49c2=25+64−2⋅5⋅8⋅21​=49, so c=7c = 7c=7.

Angle from the sides

cos⁡C=a2+b2−c22ab\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}cosC=2aba2+b2−c2​

The idea

Solve the law of cosines for cos⁡C\cos CcosC. The sign tells the shape: positive means CCC is acute, 0 means right, negative means obtuse. The largest angle is opposite the largest side — check that one to classify the triangle.

Worked example

Sides 3, 4, 5: the angle opposite 5 has cos⁡C=9+16−2524=0\cos C = \tfrac{9 + 16 - 25}{24} = 0cosC=249+16−25​=0, so it is a right angle — Pythagoras again.

Area

S=12absin⁡C=abc4RS = \tfrac12 ab\sin C = \frac{abc}{4R}S=21​absinC=4Rabc​

Symbols: SSS: the area; RRR: the circumradius (radius of the circle through AAA, BBB, CCC).

The idea

Base aaa, and the height from the third vertex is bsin⁡Cb\sin CbsinC. So the area is half of two sides times the sine of the angle between them — no need to compute the height separately.

Worked example

Two sides 6 and 8 with 30∘30^\circ30∘ between them: S=12⋅6⋅8⋅12=12S = \tfrac12\cdot 6\cdot 8\cdot\tfrac12 = 12S=21​⋅6⋅8⋅21​=12.

Ambiguous case (SSA)

sin⁡B=bsin⁡Aa\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a}sinB=absinA​

Can give 000, 111 or 222 triangles: BBB and 180∘−B180^\circ - B180∘−B.

The idea

Knowing two sides and an angle that is not between them, the law of sines gives sin⁡B\sin BsinB. Then: if sin⁡B>1\sin B > 1sinB>1 there is no triangle; if sin⁡B=1\sin B = 1sinB=1 exactly one (right angle); if sin⁡B<1\sin B < 1sinB<1 both BBB and 180∘−B180^\circ - B180∘−B may work — keep each one only if the angles still add up to less than 180∘180^\circ180∘.

Worked example

A=30∘A = 30^\circA=30∘, a=6a = 6a=6, b=8b = 8b=8: sin⁡B=8⋅126=23\sin B = \tfrac{8\cdot\tfrac12}{6} = \tfrac23sinB=68⋅21​​=32​, so B≈41.8∘B \approx 41.8^\circB≈41.8∘ or B≈138.2∘B \approx 138.2^\circB≈138.2∘. Both leave room for CCC (30+138.2<18030 + 138.2 < 18030+138.2<180): two triangles.

Sinusoids

General sinusoid

y=Asin⁡(ωx+φ)+Dy = A\sin(\omega x + \varphi) + Dy=Asin(ωx+φ)+D

Amplitude ∣A∣\lvert A\rvert∣A∣, period 2πω\tfrac{2\pi}{\omega}ω2π​, phase shift −φω-\tfrac{\varphi}{\omega}−ωφ​, midline y=Dy = Dy=D.

Symbols: ω\omegaω (omega): the angular frequency, φ\varphiφ (phi): the phase.

The idea

Each letter does one job. AAA stretches vertically (amplitude ∣A∣\lvert A\rvert∣A∣), ω\omegaω squeezes horizontally (period 2πω\tfrac{2\pi}\omegaω2π​), φ\varphiφ shifts sideways (by −φω-\tfrac\varphi\omega−ωφ​), and DDD lifts the midline. Max is D+∣A∣D + \lvert A\rvertD+∣A∣, min is D−∣A∣D - \lvert A\rvertD−∣A∣.

Worked example

y=3sin⁡(2x−π2)+1y = 3\sin(2x - \tfrac\pi2) + 1y=3sin(2x−2π​)+1: amplitude 3, period 2π2=π\tfrac{2\pi}2 = \pi22π​=π, shifted right by π4\tfrac\pi44π​, midline y=1y = 1y=1, so it goes from −2-2−2 to 444.

Combining sine and cosine

asin⁡x+bcos⁡x=Rsin⁡(x+φ)a\sin x + b\cos x = R\sin(x + \varphi)asinx+bcosx=Rsin(x+φ)R=a2+b2R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}R=a2+b2​

cos⁡φ=aR\cos\varphi = \tfrac aRcosφ=Ra​, sin⁡φ=bR\sin\varphi = \tfrac bRsinφ=Rb​. Maximum RRR, minimum −R-R−R.

Symbols: RRR here is the amplitude of the combined wave, and φ\varphiφ (phi) its phase.

The idea

A sine plus a cosine of the same angle is always a single shifted sine wave. Its amplitude is R=a2+b2R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}R=a2+b2​, so the maximum is RRR and the minimum −R-R−R — the standard way to find the extreme values of asin⁡x+bcos⁡xa\sin x + b\cos xasinx+bcosx.

Worked example

sin⁡x+3cos⁡x\sin x + \sqrt3\cos xsinx+3​cosx: R=1+3=2R = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2R=1+3​=2, cos⁡φ=12\cos\varphi = \tfrac12cosφ=21​ and sin⁡φ=32\sin\varphi = \tfrac{\sqrt3}2sinφ=23​​, so φ=π3\varphi = \tfrac\pi3φ=3π​ and the expression equals 2sin⁡(x+π3)2\sin(x + \tfrac\pi3)2sin(x+3π​), between −2-2−2 and 222.

Equations and inverse functions

sin x = a

x=arcsin⁡a+2kπx = \arcsin a + 2k\pix=arcsina+2kπx=π−arcsin⁡a+2kπx = \pi - \arcsin a + 2k\pix=π−arcsina+2kπ

Symbols: kkk: any integer (k∈Zk \in \mathbb Zk∈Z); arcsin⁡a\arcsin aarcsina: the angle in [−π2,π2][-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2][−2π​,2π​] whose sine is aaa.

The idea

The horizontal line y=ay = ay=a cuts each wave of the sine twice: at arcsin⁡a\arcsin aarcsina and at its mirror π−arcsin⁡a\pi - \arcsin aπ−arcsina. Then every full turn 2kπ2k\pi2kπ repeats them. Always look for both families.

Worked example

sin⁡x=12\sin x = \tfrac12sinx=21​ on [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π): arcsin⁡12=π6\arcsin\tfrac12 = \tfrac\pi6arcsin21​=6π​ and π−π6=5π6\pi - \tfrac\pi6 = \tfrac{5\pi}6π−6π​=65π​. These are the two crossings shown on the graph.

cos x = a

x=±arccos⁡a+2kπx = \pm\arccos a + 2k\pix=±arccosa+2kπ

Symbols: kkk: any integer; arccos⁡a\arccos aarccosa: the angle in [0,π][0, \pi][0,π] whose cosine is aaa.

The idea

Cosine is even, so the two solutions are mirror images across the yyy-axis: ±arccos⁡a\pm\arccos a±arccosa, plus full turns. In [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π) write −arccos⁡a-\arccos a−arccosa as 2π−arccos⁡a2\pi - \arccos a2π−arccosa.

cos⁡x=12\cos x = \tfrac12cosx=21​: arccos⁡12=π3\arccos\tfrac12 = \tfrac\pi3arccos21​=3π​, so x=π3x = \tfrac\pi3x=3π​ or x=2π−π3=5π3x = 2\pi - \tfrac\pi3 = \tfrac{5\pi}3x=2π−3π​=35π​ in [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π).

tan x = a

x=arctan⁡a+kπx = \arctan a + k\pix=arctana+kπ

Symbols: kkk: any integer; arctan⁡a\arctan aarctana: the angle in (−π2,π2)(-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2)(−2π​,2π​) whose tangent is aaa.

The idea

Tangent takes every value exactly once per period π\piπ, so there is a single family: arctan⁡a+kπ\arctan a + k\piarctana+kπ. In [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π) that gives two solutions, half a turn apart.

tan⁡x=1\tan x = 1tanx=1: arctan⁡1=π4\arctan 1 = \tfrac\pi4arctan1=4π​, so x=π4x = \tfrac\pi4x=4π​ and x=π4+π=5π4x = \tfrac\pi4 + \pi = \tfrac{5\pi}4x=4π​+π=45π​ in [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π).

Ranges

arcsin⁡∈[−π2,π2]\arcsin \in \left[-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2\right]arcsin∈[−2π​,2π​]arccos⁡∈[0,π]\arccos \in [0, \pi]arccos∈[0,π]arctan⁡∈(−π2,π2)\arctan \in \left(-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2\right)arctan∈(−2π​,2π​)

The idea

arcsin⁡\arcsinarcsin, arccos⁡\arccosarccos and arctan⁡\arctanarctan return one chosen angle, always in a fixed interval. So arcsin⁡(sin⁡x)=x\arcsin(\sin x) = xarcsin(sinx)=x only when xxx is already in [−π2,π2][-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2][−2π​,2π​]; otherwise find the angle in that interval with the same sine.

Worked example

arcsin⁡(sin⁡3π4)\arcsin(\sin\tfrac{3\pi}4)arcsin(sin43π​): sin⁡3π4=22\sin\tfrac{3\pi}4 = \tfrac{\sqrt2}2sin43π​=22​​, and the angle in [−π2,π2][-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2][−2π​,2π​] with that sine is π4\tfrac\pi44π​ — not 3π4\tfrac{3\pi}443π​.

Useful identity

arcsin⁡x+arccos⁡x=π2\arcsin x + \arccos x = \frac\pi2arcsinx+arccosx=2π​

The idea

If sin⁡α=x\sin\alpha = xsinα=x, then the complementary angle π2−α\tfrac\pi2 - \alpha2π​−α has cosine xxx. So the angle whose sine is xxx and the angle whose cosine is xxx always add up to a right angle.

Worked example

arcsin⁡12+arccos⁡12=π6+π3=π2\arcsin\tfrac12 + \arccos\tfrac12 = \tfrac\pi6 + \tfrac\pi3 = \tfrac\pi2arcsin21​+arccos21​=6π​+3π​=2π​. The green line on the graph is constant: the sum never changes.
